Fitbit has completely ruined what used to be one of its best features. The new sleep scoring system is inconsistent, overly punitive, and often doesn’t reflect how well I actually slept. I’ve had nights with excellent dreams, solid REM and deep sleep, and woken up feeling fantastic, only to receive a mediocre rating. Under the previous system, these same nights would typically score around 80–81.

The new algorithm seems to penalize certain sleep patterns excessively while ignoring how rested users actually feel. I’ve used Fitbit long enough to recognize the difference, and this change has made the sleep score significantly less useful.

Please bring back the previous scoring system, or at least give users the option to choose between the old and new versions. This is a major step backward.

reviews.title: Lost All Credibility
reviews.text: I have been increasingly disappointed with Fitbit since its integration with Google Health. What was once a reliable and user-friendly fitness tracker has become frustrating and unreliable. I keep experiencing errors and inaccuracies in my health and activity data, and despite these problems, issues remain unresolved consistently when submitting feedback. I am clearly not alone as many other users I know are reporting similar problems, including inaccurate sleep tracking, incorrect step counts, unreliable workout and heart rate readings, syncing problems, missing data and rapidly draining batteries. The new app is also less intuitive, cluttered and harder to navigate, with unwanted AI features taking priority over the basic information users actually want. What is particularly disappointing is the lack of meaningful fixes and customer support. Fitbit built its reputation on reliability and simplicity, but that seems to have been lost under Google. The software… lets start with the vitals. RHR and HRV can both be green and within range, however if RHR is below 60 the algo will always rate it POOR/FAIR. HRV can also be within range but a single digit change will also rate it poorly. This nukes your daily readiness and resilience score persistently. Which is extremely frustrating as someone who’s heart rate is lower due to a good level of fitness. If you’re the type of person who likes to see a good day pay off in that score don’t buy this. 

Once the algo has crunched your numbers for the day, maybe you get up for some water, it will stick to its calculation for the day. If you then go back to bed, sleep more, it will not take any of this into account. The calculation is complete and that’s that. Live with it. 

The dashboard is OK. It’s very unintuitive as holding to rearrange segments is not possible. Expanding the dashboard is impossible if you’d like to see more. 

There is an excellent product in here somewhere… atm I’m extremely close to selling it and going back to something else that has the software refined to the basic level required. ATM it’s trash.

reviews.title: Potential is massive, Execution is disappointing
reviews.text:
I recently switched from an Apple Watch to the Fitbit Air and Google Health. I wanted something discreet that I could wear without constant notifications and distractions, that tracked all the metrics I’m interested in and, most importantly, didn’t need charging every other day.

For the most part, the Fitbit Air delivers on that promise. Unfortunately, it doesn’t work properly on my tattooed arm, which is disappointing. :(

What excited me most about moving to Google Health was the prospect of having everything in one place: health data, training plans, workout tracking and calorie tracking, rather than having to juggle multiple apps. My Fitbit came with three months of Google Health Premium, so I’ve been giving the whole ecosystem a fair chance.

On the surface, I like it. There’s plenty of data to explore, and I enjoy the insights it provides, even if certain metrics, like Resilience, seem completely impossible to move! However, I’ve noticed some significant differences compared with my Apple Watch. My resting heart rate, previously in the low-to-mid 50s, is now showing in the low-to-mid 60s, while my HRV has dropped from consistently being in the 100s to somewhere between 50 and 80. I appreciate that different devices can use different algorithms, but it does leave me questioning which readings are the most accurate.

The user interface is another disappointment. For a company like Google, the overall experience feels surprisingly basic, uninspiring and lacking in polish.

Second- the coach aspect seems to be geared more toward newer to fitness individuals. It is overall unhelpful to people that have more experience in this area. It frequently prioritizes walking, swimming or other rest day activities. The overall fitness programming could use some work as well. I’ve entered my information and set it to know that I am certified in all the fitness things and create my own programming yet it still keeps trying to recommend too easy or rest day workouts. I also have to keep “reminding” the AI helper of things I’ve already said because it will frequently repeat nonrelevant or outdated information. 
Overall the idea is cool, and it’s great for beginners on their fitness journey. But if you already have a good knowledge of what you’re doing, I wouldn’t recommend paying extra for the coach aspect and just use it as your basic Fitbit wearable. The AI is not as advanced as other AI’s at this time. It can get really annoying.

reviews.title: Fitbit Air: Zero Sleep Is Not Missing Data
reviews.text: Due to a medical condition, I often cannot sleep without prescribed sleep medication. Because I do not take it every day, my established sleep pattern is often to sleep every other day and sleep longer on the days when I do sleep. I previously used older Fitbit models, including a 3-series device and a Fitbit 5, and both handled this pattern properly. However, my new Fitbit Air now says, “No sleep was detected” and asks me to manually enter my sleep. This prompt is illogical and extremely frustrating: I cannot manually enter a sleep period that never occurred. The Air was worn continuously and recorded my other health and activity data, so a genuinely sleepless day should be recorded as 0 hours of sleep—not treated as missing data. Zero is not the same as null. Excluding zero-sleep days makes the average sleep statistic mathematically invalid for people with severe insomnia or irregular sleep patterns. For example, if I sleep 14 hours one day and 0 hours the next, my true daily average is 7 hours; if the zero-sleep day is omitted, Fitbit incorrectly reports an average of 14 hours and completely reverses my actual health pattern. Please restore the behavior available with older Fitbit devices, add an explicit “No sleep / 0 hours” state, include confirmed sleepless days in calendar-day averages, and stop asking users to manually log sleep that did not happen.

Ask yourself why most average people buy a Fitbit - they want to easily track their steps/activity minutes/distance/calorie burn. That is therefore the info that needs to be front and centre in the app, not just that day, but for the long term. Like it used to be when it was Fitbit. Not buried somewhere like it is now. In developing the new app, you’ve tried to make it fancy but not stopped to think what people want and their objective of using it and therefore you’ve lost your key audience. Unless this is charged and improved, I’m highly unlikely to buy another Fitbit when this one comes to the end of its life

I’ve been a Fitbit user for over 10 years and was generally happy with both the devices and the Fitbit app. Unfortunately, the transition to Google Health has been a major step backwards.
The new app makes basic tasks unnecessarily difficult. Food logging is far less intuitive than it used to be, requiring more taps and searches to enter meals. Something that was once quick and effortless now feels frustrating and time-consuming - I had to move to MyFitnessPal instead. 
Managing personal health data is also surprisingly awkward. Editing or deleting weight entries is not straightforward, and correcting mistakes feels far more complicated than it should be. For a health-tracking app, users need simple and reliable control over their own data.
The biggest disappointment is that years of historical Fitbit data are now tied to an experience that is significantly worse than the original Fitbit app. Long-term users who helped build the Fitbit ecosystem deserve a better migration experience and a more user-friendly app.
I hope Google listens to feedback and restores the simplicity and usability that made Fitbit so popular in the first place.

reviews.text: Having been a Fitbit user for many, many years, change was always going to inevitably be difficult. However, I was prepared to embrace this change with the hope that the backing of Google would lead to a fresh interface and major updates to the features available. That is certainly what Google delivered, but in all the wrong ways. The dashboard occupies at best 25% of your phone screen, making it very minimalist and functional. This is Google’s MO, but not what I want from my fitness app. Like most users, I want a simple, pleasing to the eye, considered user interface. Unfortunately Apple have had Google beat in this arena for decades and I don’t see that changing anytime soon. With regard to functionality, I’ve never seen so many bugs or lost features in my life. This clearly feels like a rushed development. Nutrition tracking has been hit the worst with information being input not equating to information output, duplications of data which resolve only when re-synced and the loss of the ability to add your own food items. This is one of those instances where Google would’ve done a much better job had they kept the old Fitbit features etc and just slapped a shiny new face on it. Let’s hope Google do some extensive work to bring this app up to par. Otherwise, despite being a buyer of Fitbit products for nearly two decades, I will be seeking an alternative device as my next product.

reviews.title: If I wanted a second job managing your AI, I would have applied for one.
reviews.text:
I am writing this review with an immense amount of irony. I am a paid Gemini subscriber, and up until recently, I was a happy Fitbit Premium subscriber. I clearly see the value in AI. But here is the thing: If I wanted my fitness tracking and my LLM subscriptions to merge, I would have asked for it.
Instead, the new Google Health app has forcibly shoved AI into every single component of the interface with absolutely no way to permanently opt out. It has completely obliterated a layout that worked perfectly fine for years.
My personalized, carefully chosen metrics? Either buried under layers of menus or completely gone. Most frustratingly, the hourly step reminder and count—a core feature of why I wear a tracker in the first place—has vanished into the ether. The app is now essentially useless if you just want to manage your health goals without an AI assistant breathing down your neck and analyzing your data through its own algorithmic lens.
The lack of user autonomy here is staggering. Forcing AI as a mandatory interface choice rather than an opt-in feature ruins the entire user experience for long-time customers.
The bottom line: My premium subscription is not getting renewed, and when my current device inevitably dies, I will not be buying another Fitbit—or whatever Google decides to rename it next week. Currently researching Apple Watches. Thanks for saving me the subscription money, I guess.

I can’t log food without having to work out whatever a cup is for a measurement - and Google Health decides when a food is measured by ‘cup’ or ‘g’ .. so if they decide you measure peas as a cup despite me weighing out 100 grams exactly, well you just have to deal with that. 

After you’ve logged anything, the pop up asking you if you want to view what you’ve just added is persistent. It just doesn’t go away until you click on it to view what you’ve just done whether you want it or not. 

There’s no option to have all your stats on a single screen - you have to swipe across even if the bottom of the screen is empty..

Frankly this feels like someone’s used Gemini to build a new app and sacked off anyone in UX and they’ll work it out later. But honestly, I’ve never felt more compelled to take the plunge and get an iwatch (with the dreadful 18hr battery…!!) because at least they get the simple things right.. 

…tbh, I probably won’t (because of the battery mostly), but I thought about it having gotten so frustrated with this frankly dreadful upgrade of a previously fairly good app 

Last thing - sleep score is still dreadful and we should still have an option to remove it from sleep stats. Give us that and I’ll bump this to a 3 star review maybe 4 🤔

reviews.title: After 8 years, I’m done
reviews.text:
I was unhappy with Fitbit all throughout my pregnancy since they won’t even acknowledge that pregnancy exists- but I had made it work by hiding and unselecting all the health goals. The main number one thing I track is my sleep. Today, Fitbit combined the app with Google Health, completely changed the entire design, and overwrote all my recent data. It’s completely worthless. 
The update said it would be a big change, but it also promised “all your data will still be there!” That is a flat out lie. Because of the nursing and night wake ups, I’ve had to manually input my sleep data for 3 months now- which was tedious, but I had time on my hands. It overwrote all that and replaced it with its own version. Now, it’s full of AI slop like “looks like you had a rough night’s sleep, listen to your body today“
I know, stupid app. I know. And the emphasis on cardio is extreme- I am not in a cardio phase of life right now. 
They have always called them “fitness trackers “ but I feel that you can now only use one if you are a gym rat. If you’re not in perfect health, then none of it applies to you and it’s actually really condescending and demeaning. If I’m not going to be able to meet a goal for another 6 months or more (when my baby is older, I imagine I’ll sleep better, surprise!!) then it’s cruel to criticize me every day until then. So now, they get all my data to sell at their leisure, and I get useless but sexy modern style charts that don’t accurately reflect reality. 
I’m out.
